stories.headline: Houthi missile hits Aramco building in Saudi Arabia, four injured in Riyadh
stories.title: Houthi missile hits Aramco building in Saudi Arabia, four injured in Riyadh
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 14: A missile launched by Yemen’s Houthi movement struck a building belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran overnight, escalating the confrontation between the Iran-backed group and the Saudi-led coalition, the BBC reported. Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said the attack caused a “limited fire” in an administrative building at Aramco’s headquarters. Saudi authorities also reported that several missiles and drones were intercepted elsewhere, while falling debris injured four people in the capital, Riyadh. The attack came after the Saudi-led coalition struck a fuel depot operated by the Yemen Petroleum Company at al-Sabaha, near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, on Tuesday. The Houthis said they had targeted Aramco and Riyadh’s airport in retaliation for the coalition’s strike and warned that further attacks would follow in the coming days. The latest escalation has further heightened concerns over the security of Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure and the potential disruption of regional oil supplies and international shipping. BBC reported that International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned that the intensifying conflict could have “potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere”. The Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, had vowed on Tuesday that the Houthis would “bear the consequences” of their recent attacks on the kingdom. The warning followed a missile strike on Riyadh’s airport on Saturday that killed 13 people including an Indian. The Houthis have also claimed responsibility for attacks targeting Saudi airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases. The group has said its attacks are retaliation for Saudi air strikes on areas under its control in western Yemen, including Sanaa. The renewed confrontation comes amid escalating fighting along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including around the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and serves as a key gateway to the Suez Canal. The growing threat to energy facilities and shipping routes has raised concerns over wider regional instability and its implications for global trade. Yemen has been engulfed in civil war since 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015 after a Saudi-led coalition intervened in support of the internationally recognised government.

stories.headline: NC manifesto hangs in balance as CM Omar-led govt completes 2 years in office tomorrow
stories.title: NC manifesto hangs in balance as CM Omar-led govt completes 2 years in office tomorrow
stories.summary: Jammu, Oct 14: They say – there’s many a slip between the cup and the lip! “Red letter day” of October 16 is just round the corner- precisely just a day away – when the incumbent elected government, led by the Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, will complete its second year in office in the Union Territory set-up of Jammu and Kashmir. So here comes the perfect appraisal time to count those slips between the “cup” and the “lip”, though not in proverbial dimensions. In the context of appraisal, “lip” will denote promises by the helmsmen and “cup” – their delivery to “the ruled”. It’s time to measure and judge to what extent “Dignity, Identity and Development” promised as a “solemn pledge” to the people reached their doorsteps. If one goes by the shriller voices in the corridors of power, statehood has remained the dominant chorus – the fulcrum of the ruling alliance of National Conference-Congress’ political juggernaut throughout the year. The plank continued to offer as an impenetrable shield to the alliance and particularly the National Conference against the opposition’s unrelenting onslaught. Unlike his reconciliatory approach during the first year in office, second year saw CM Omar stridently fighting, protesting for restoration of statehood and projecting that its (statehood’s) absence only caused all the “slips” between the “cup” and the “lip” to blunt opposition’s offensive vis-à-vis non fulfilment of poll promises (by NC). Interestingly, the government, fully aware of harsh realities of politics, during its second year in power, has less relied on its trite plank during first one year that its mandate to fulfil poll promises is for five years and not one, two or three years - to duck prickly queries of both the opposition and the people. As a sagacious old player in the political arena, it has focussed more on “absence of statehood” to shift the burden of its “complete failure in governance”, (as alleged by its detractors), on its political opponents (read BJP only) as well. But does it convince the opposition, which has already written off the NC-led alliance government as “Failed” consecutively in its second Annual Performance Report (APR) or the people – the ruled? Absolutely not – in case of opposition! In the case of people, nothing can be said with certainty as they actually speak only after five years through votes! To be fair, it (NC government) has tried to take baby- steps towards the realisation of several of its promises made in its manifesto. Though it’s a story for another day that most of those steps, so far, have proved to be nothing more than paper-horses – the distance between the cup and the lip persists. Keeping the “paper-horses” proposition in mind, one can tick mark the boxes while sifting through its 12 guarantees, as mentioned in NC manifesto 2024. With regard to its first guarantee related to “Restoration of political and legal status” – it continues to strive for “full implementation of autonomy resolution”; “restoration of Articles 370 and 35 A” and statehood as prior to August 5, 2019. The government has kept its promise – it is striving for all three “big guarantees.” But how will it continue to strive for them? None has any idea and even the government, itself, is clueless. In any case, except statehood, two other guarantees can justifiably be not part of the government's real APR (other than the wordy duel). However, it kept its word to move resolutions in the assembly and get them passed. While it succeeded in reviving its autonomy resolution of 2000 in the just concluded autumn session of J&K Legislature, the words Articles 370 and 35-A could not see their verbatim entry in any of resolutions passed so far by the House or the J&K Council of Ministers. Cornered by the opposition in this context, the government maintained that the word “special status” mentioned in the resolutions was their (Articles 370 n 35-A’s) cloak. It had promised to make endeavours to redraw the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 and the transaction of Business of the Government of Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir Rules, 2019. As promised, its endeavours continued even when it’s about to complete its second year in office. “Files remained pending with the Centre,” the government reaffirms. The status of files related to tweaking of reservation rules (policy), committee report about regularisation of daily wagers too remains in knowledge of government only. Opaqueness persists about the efforts to “modify, annul and repeal post August 5, 2019 laws impacting J&K’s special status”; “protect the land and employment rights of the people of J&K” and “secure the release of prisoners languishing in jails.” But as they are some tricky propositions, it will be fair enough to push their APR to 2029. Similar is the status about the guarantee to repeal the Public Safety Act (PSA). One can wait for these guarantees to fructify, even after 2029. But the opposition and people can genuinely question the status of guarantee to “fill up all vacancies in government departments within 180 days” and realisation of other related promises on the ground (beyond announcement and flurry of paper horses). Next guarantee related to “200 units of electricity free”. In the manifesto, there were no strings attached to it. But in the current scenario, as opposition, too, repeatedly targets – the government has shifted its “goal post to AAY families” and now it is linked to “PM Surya GharMuftBijliYojana” of Government of India. Moving on, does anyone remember that the party has given a guarantee to “provide Rs 5000 per month to female heads of EWS households”? If not, forget it. EWS (families) to get 12 cylinders free of cost per year - was another guarantee. The government, in its second year, endeavoured to fulfil this promise partially and with “strings attached.” It has kept its promises to enhance the old age and widow pension, free ride for women (with partial tweaking) in e-buses and free education (for all) with a tweaked proposition. It has been successful in restoration of Darbar Move in its second year. The government has maintained that it has also fulfilled its poll promise related to “Ease of Doing Business” with the passage of a related bill in the just concluded autumn session. Rest of its major guarantees and promises remain out of its own realm so far and this gives the opposition a handle to beat it, in an unrelenting manner. “How dual power is creating obstruction in good governance? On statehood, earlier NC (other parties’) stance was - it would come on its own and we will have to wage a bigger war for Art 370 and 35 A. Youth continue to be incarcerated in jails outside J&K. What has happened to 12 free cylinders to all? There were certain achievable goals even within the UT setup, they (NC government) could not get them even,” maintains former minister and senior leader of J&K Apni Party, G H Mir, while talking to GKTV. He claimed that in 1983, NC in its manifesto had promised to ensure posts for Chief Secretary, DGP and Chief Justice for J&K citizens but after coming to power, it brought Chief Secretary from outside. “When there was statehood, they wanted autonomy. In the current scenario, they are seeking statehood. It simply means they don’t want to deliver. We too support statehood demand. But their (NC’s) politics always revolves around exploitation of people’s sentiments by provoking them against the Centre and not good governance. They are now resorting to confrontational politics. Confrontation is not going to help it, anyway. It did not help in the past, it will not help even now,” Mir points out. “The election happened under the UT setup to govern a Union Territory. The Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, himself, was on record saying that he had served as the Chief Minister of State so it would be embarrassing for him to contest for power in UT. But he did and won power. However, he could not effectively use powers even within the UT set up to make people’s life better. Dual power is a system prevalent at many places but it cannot be used as an excuse to deprive the people of good governance or one promised to them (people) while contesting for UT. How is the dual system obstructing filling of vacant posts,” former minister argues. Leader of the Opposition in J&K Legislature Sunil Sharma too has repeatedly targeted the government for using “statehood” as a plank to “cover-up its failure to fulfil poll promises.” “Corruption has become deeply entrenched under the present dispensation, while transparency and accountability have been completely sidelined. The government's policy of outsourcing jobs without establishing a transparent and foolproof recruitment mechanism,” he alleges, adding, “Such policies created ample space for manipulation, favouritism and corruption while depriving deserving youth of fair employment opportunities.” J&K BJP leadership also criticises NC government, for what it alleges, “deliberately resorting to dirty tactics to delay Panchayat elections, weaken the Panchayati Raj Institutions and obstruct the functioning of the three-tier democratic system in Jammu and Kashmir.” “The grassroots democracy could not be sacrificed for political convenience,” BJP leaders assert.

stories.headline: Rajasthan Awards Single Largest Solar-Plus-BESS Tender 2.45 GW at Rs. 3.53–3.54/kWh
stories.title: Rajasthan Awards Single Largest Solar-Plus-BESS Tender 2.45 GW at Rs. 3.53–3.54/kWh
stories.summary: After around nine months of issuing one of its largest solar-plus-battery energy storage system (BESS) tenders, Rajasthan Solar Park Development Company Limited (RSDCL) has awarded 2,450 MW of solar capacity paired with 1,600 MW/6,400 MWh of energy storage systems (ESS) at tariffs of Rs. 3.53–3.54/kWh. Around 35 bidders participated in the tender issued by RSDCL, but only three bidders won this project around nine months after the tender was issued in January this year. Three bidders emerged as winners: NLC India Renewable Energy (NIRL), the renewable energy arm of NLC India; Rama Reflection India Pvt. Ltd.; and Coal India Ltd. NLC India secured a 1,000 MW solar-plus-BESS project at Pugal Solar Park, securing the largest individual project allocation. At the same tariff, Rama Reflection won a 250 MW solar project 660 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS). Coal India also won a 1,000 MW solar-plus-BESS project at a slightly higher tariff of Rs. 3.54/kWh. The company has previously secured a BESS project from Telangana Power Generation Corporation Limited ( TSGENCO ) at Choutuppal, comprising 187.5 MW/750 MWh of storage capacity with a four-hour discharge duration. The project was awarded at a tariff of Rs. 3.14 lakh/MW/month. Scope of Work Under the scope of work, Rajasthan Renewable Energy Corporation Ltd. ( RRECL ) plans to develop the project across eight plots of 250 MW each, aggregating 2,000 MW. RSDCL issued the tender for project development on a Build-Own-Operate (BOO) basis. The developer must ensure an annual Capacity Utilisation Factor (CUF) of no more than 28%, in line with Rajasthan Urja Vikas and IT Services Limited's (RUVITL) commitment to procure energy up to this annual CUF in each contract year. Under the tender, RUVITL will enter into Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with the successful bidders on behalf of the state's distribution companies: Jaipur Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited (JVVNL), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited (AVVNL), and Jodhpur Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited (JDVVNL). The original tender covered up to 2,450 MW of solar capacity, divided into two lots. Lot 1 comprised 2,000 MW of solar capacity paired with 1,320 MW/5,280 MWh of BESS. Lot 2 covered 450 MW of solar capacity paired with 280 MW/1,120 MWh of BESS, to be developed across two plots of 225 MW each.

article_sentences: Indian shares are set to open lower on Thursday, tracking Asian peers as a quicker-than-expected increase in US consumer price inflation raised expectations of another rate hike by the Federal Reserve this year.

Higher US rates make emerging markets such as India less attractive for overseas investors, who have already sold Indian stocks for 14 straight sessions into Wednesday, taking year-to-date outflows to a record $32.7 billion.
GIFT Nifty futures were at 22,606.5 at 7:52 a.m. IST, indicating a negative start for the benchmark Nifty 50, which closed at 22,622.7 on Wednesday.
Hotter-than-expected US inflation reinforces concerns over tighter global monetary conditions, a sentimental negative for risk assets such as emerging market equities, two traders said.
Domestic investor attention is likely to remain focused on company earnings, with Wipro scheduled to report its second-quarter results later in the day.

Following HCL Tech's better-than-expected earnings earlier this week, which sparked a rally in technology stocks, markets will closely scrutinize Wipro's outlook for discretionary technology spending, deal conversions and margins.
Robust primary-market activity could continue to divert liquidity from the secondary market, potentially limiting near-term upside for stocks, two traders said.
Jio Platforms on Wednesday announced plans to raise up to $3.2 billion in what would be India's largest initial public offering to date.
The IPO would value the Mukesh Ambani-founded group at about $108.3 billion, with a price band of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 Indian rupees ($11.19 to $11.76) per share.

stories.headline: Kashmirification of Delhi
stories.title: Kashmirification of Delhi
stories.summary: There is something profoundly revealing about the images emerging from New Delhi ahead of the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar. Barricaded roads, restrictions on movement, suspended internet services, cancelled trains, detained students and a massive deployment of security personnel. A national capital preparing to contain its own citizens raises a question that should trouble every believer in constitutional democracy: why does a government that derives its authority from the people appear so apprehensive when those very people assemble to question it? For Kashmiris, this spectacle is not unfamiliar. It is a reminder of August 2019, when Jammu and Kashmir was placed under sweeping restrictions, communication networks were shut down and political life was profoundly disrupted as the Union Government proceeded to abrogate Article 370 and reorganise the state. What Delhi is reportedly experiencing today, Kashmir has known for years. The difference is that Kashmiris were expected to accept it as normal. What happened to Kashmir in 2019? On 5 August 2019, the constitutional changes relating to Article 370 were announced. Parliament subsequently passed the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, which came into effect on 31 October 2019. The former state was divided into two Union Territories, Jammu and Kashmir with a legislature and Ladakh without one. Consider the magnitude of this transformation. A full fledged state, with its own elected legislature and constitutional arrangements, ceased to exist in its previous form. Its political status was fundamentally altered. Its territory was reorganised. Its people were placed under a new administrative arrangement in which the Union Government acquired a substantially more direct role in governance. And what was the condition in which this transformation unfolded? Communications had been suspended, restrictions on movement and public gatherings had been imposed, and political leaders had been detained. The Supreme Court’s judgment in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, delivered in January 2020, records the communication restrictions and examines the constitutional limits on such measures. What does it mean for democracy when a decision of such extraordinary political consequence is implemented while the population most directly affected faces severe restrictions on communication and assembly? Can a people meaningfully participate in a debate about their political future when their ability to communicate, organise and protest is curtailed? These are not questions that disappear because Parliament has passed a law. They are questions about democratic legitimacy, accountability and the relationship between power and consent. Who governs, and who gets to decide? The central question is not merely whether a government possesses legal authority to take a particular decision. It is whether the exercise of that authority respects the democratic principles that give constitutional power its legitimacy. Karl Marx examined the relationship between political institutions and the distribution of power in society. His central insight was that political arrangements cannot be understood merely by examining their formal structures. One must also ask who exercises power, whose interests those arrangements serve and who bears the consequences. Applied to Kashmir, this perspective forces us to ask uncomfortable questions. Who gained greater control over the administration of Jammu and Kashmir after 2019? Who lost the political authority that comes with statehood? Who had the final say over the future of the region, and how much meaningful influence did its people exercise over that decision? Statehood is not simply a label on a government building. It represents a distribution of constitutional authority. A state government operates within the federal structure with powers and responsibilities distinct from those of a Union Territory administration. The transition to Union Territory status changed the institutional balance between elected representatives and the Union Government. To call this a mere administrative reorganisation is to overlook the political substance of what occurred. And if the argument was that these changes would ultimately benefit the people of Jammu and Kashmir, should those people not be entitled to ask when their statehood will be restored? The promise of statehood cannot remain indefinite In December 2023, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional changes concerning Article 370. It directed that Assembly elections be conducted by 30 September 2024 and stated that statehood should be restored at the earliest and as soon as possible. Assembly elections were subsequently held in 2024, and Jammu and Kashmir now has an elected government. Yet restoration of statehood remains a distinct and consequential question. The distinction matters. An elected Assembly is essential to representative government, but it does not make a Union Territory equivalent to a state. Nor does the holding of elections, by itself, answer the question of when the constitutional status of statehood will be restored. If elections have taken place, what is the justification for leaving the restoration of statehood without a definite political conclusion? If democratic normalcy is the objective, why should the return of a fuller measure of statehood remain a promise whose fulfilment is still awaited? A people should not have to repeatedly ask whether the constitutional position they once enjoyed will ever be restored. Nor should democratic participation be reduced to casting a vote while the larger question of political authority remains unresolved. The demand for statehood is therefore not merely an administrative demand. It is a demand for a clearer balance of power, greater democratic accountability and respect for the political aspirations of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. Kashmir warned India. Did India listen? For years, Kashmiris have spoken about communication blackouts, restrictions on movement, preventive detention and the narrowing space for political dissent. We have argued that extraordinary powers, once normalised in one region, can reshape the expectations of governance elsewhere. Yet Kashmir was frequently treated as an exception. Its circumstances were invoked to justify restrictions that many outside the region could scarcely imagine experiencing in their own lives. Its political grievances were often reduced to questions of security, while its demands for democratic rights were viewed through suspicion. That distinction was always dangerous. A constitutional right cannot depend on the geography of the person exercising it. Freedom of expression does not become less valuable in Srinagar than in Delhi. The right to assemble peacefully does not acquire a different constitutional meaning when exercised by Kashmiri students rather than students in the national capital. If restrictions in Delhi are as extensive as reported, the relevant questions must be asked openly. What specific threat justifies each restriction? Are the measures necessary and proportionate? Could less restrictive alternatives protect public order? Are citizens being prevented from exercising their rights simply because the authorities anticipate opposition? A democracy cannot answer these questions by invoking security in the abstract. Restrictions must be justified by evidence and assessed against constitutional standards. Is Delhi becoming what Kashmir was made to endure? The comparison between Kashmir in 2019 and Delhi today should not be mistaken for a claim that the two situations are identical. Their legal contexts, security circumstances and political histories differ. But the reported restrictions in Delhi evoke a troubling pattern that Kashmiris recognise: the use of extraordinary administrative and security measures to control the possibility of mass political expression. That is what makes the phrase Kashmirification of Delhi so politically significant. The issue is not that Delhi has suddenly become Kashmir in every respect. The issue is that methods once associated with the exceptional treatment of Kashmir are now being discussed in relation to the national capital. The question is whether the normalisation of such methods has weakened the safeguards that ought to protect every citizen. An emergency like atmosphere need not be declared a formal Emergency to warrant scrutiny. The suspension of ordinary freedoms, the containment of dissent and the expansion of executive control can create a democratic crisis even when constitutional institutions continue to function. Elections alone cannot settle the question. A government may win an electoral mandate and still be required to justify its restrictions, answer criticism and respect the rights of its opponents. The purpose of democracy is not to make governments comfortable. It is to make power accountable. The test of India’s democracy Kashmir has never asked for its people to be treated as an exception to India’s constitutional promises. It has asked that those promises be honoured. It has asked that its political future not be treated as a matter exclusively for distant authorities. It has asked for statehood, accountable government and the dignity of meaningful democratic participation. If the rest of India is now confronting questions that Kashmir has raised for years, will it finally listen? Will the national conversation recognise that the rights of Kashmiris were never merely a regional concern? Will institutions insist that restrictions on peaceful assembly and communication be justified under the Constitution, regardless of where they occur? Will the restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood be treated as a serious democratic commitment rather than an indefinitely deferred assurance? And, above all, what kind of democracy are we building if the state responds to citizens demanding answers by making it increasingly difficult for them to be heard? The barricades around Jantar Mantar may eventually come down. Internet services may resume, trains may return to their schedules and security personnel may leave the streets. But these developments alone will not resolve the deeper questions raised by the episode. Nor will they erase what Kashmir experienced in 2019. For Kashmiris, the lesson is painfully familiar. Democracy can be weakened not only by the cancellation of elections, but also by the gradual erosion of the freedoms that make elections meaningful. It can be diminished when political power becomes increasingly centralised, when dissent is treated as disruption and when a population is asked to accept decisions about its future without adequate space to challenge them. A government that believes in the strength of its democratic mandate should not fear questions from its citizens. And a country that believes in constitutional democracy must be willing to confront an uncomfortable truth: the freedoms it protects in its capital cannot be separated from the freedoms it permits in its peripheries. In 2019, Kashmir was told to accept a new political reality. Today, as Delhi confronts the possibility of extraordinary restrictions on protest, India must ask itself whether it is prepared to defend the democratic principles that Kashmiris insisted were never theirs alone. If the silencing of Kashmir was once treated as an exception, and similar methods are now a source of national concern, how long can India continue to ignore the warning? Adv Shriya Handoo, Research Head and Spokesperson, JKNC

stories.headline: Historic Shah Kul: HC seeks updated report on demarcation, removal of encroachments
stories.title: Historic Shah Kul: HC seeks updated report on demarcation, removal of encroachments
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 14: The High Court of J&K and Ladakh has granted the authorities 10 more days to complete the ongoing demarcation and removal of encroachments from the Shah Kul -- a historical canal of importance and a national monument that had been the main source of water to Nishat Gardens since the time of Mughal Emperor Jahangir. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Dr Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajesh Sekhri directed the authorities to submit a report updating the status of demarcation and removal of encroachments on the Shah Kul by October 27. The Court was hearing a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by Mir Muhammad Shafi in 2023, seeking restoration of the centuries-old canal and removal of encroachments from its original alignment. During the proceeding, the court’s attention was drawn to the divisional commissioner Kashmir’s status report indicating constitution of a committee comprising the Deputy Commissioner, Srinagar; Vice Chairman, Lakes Conservation and Management Authority (LCMA); Regional Director, Survey and Land Records (Central), Srinagar; and Superintending Engineer, Irrigation and Flood Control, Srinagar. The committee formed pursuant to the September 15 order, has been tasked with consolidating the list of encroachments after proper demarcation with reference to revenue records, examining claims regarding property rights and preparing a time-bound action plan for removal of identified encroachments and restoration of Shah Kul. The Court was informed that the demarcation exercise had commenced and that voluntary removal as well as time-bound removal of encroachments was being undertaken simultaneously. It was also told that around 47 structures broadly fell within the scope of encroachment. Of these, 28 structures have so far been demarcated, while around 20 have already been removed. The remaining eight demarcated structures are likely to be removed shortly, they informed the court. Furthermore, the authorities further submitted that once the demarcation exercise is completed, any encroachers who fail to remove the structures voluntarily would face removal during an anti-encroachment drive. Allowing the 10-day time sought by them, the Bench directed the authorities to update the Court on the progress made in the demarcation and removal exercise.

stories.title: Supreme Court upholds Madras HC order quashing Tamil Nadu reservation notification for converts to Islam
stories.summary: The court held that a Tamil Nadu government order doing the same creates an “artificial group” which would access benefits of reservation associated with backward communities
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Supreme Court of India on Thursday (October 15, 2026) rejected a Tamil Nadu government appeal seeking confirmation of the State’s policy to provide reservation benefits to members of backward classes, most backward classes, de-notified communities and Scheduled Castes to Islam.

A Bench headed by Justice Prashant Kumar Mishra held that a member of a backward Hindu community does not automatically become a member of a notified backward Muslim community merely by going through the act of conversion to Islam.
The court held that a Tamil Nadu government order doing the same creates an “artificial group” which would access benefits of reservation associated with backward communities.

Justice Mishra, who read out the operative portion of the judgment, said the government’s notification of a community as backward for granting them benefits should be preceded by statutory social checks.

New Delhi: The Centre has defended its decision to suspend mobile internet services in parts of central Delhi ahead of the October 10 protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, telling the Supreme Court that the restriction was necessary to maintain public order.
Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan has tendered an unconditional apology to the court after receiving a contempt notice over alleged non-compliance with its directions concerning the restrictions.
In a counter-affidavit filed late on Wednesday, Mohan maintained that the 24-hour suspension was a proportionate response to security concerns raised by Delhi.

The Centre has also sought a modification of the Supreme Court's October 11 order to permit internet suspensions when necessary, subject to legal requirements and safeguards.
The government denied that the shutdown amounted to a wilful violation of the court's directions and sought relief from the contempt proceedings against the Home Secretary.
Why did the Centre suspend internet services in Delhi?
According to the affidavit, mobile internet services were suspended from 10 pm on October 9 to 10 pm on October 10 within a four-kilometre radius of Raisina Hill.
Mohan said the decision followed a request from Delhi.

stories.headline: Medical fraternity must bridge urban-rural healthcare gaps: LG Sinha
stories.title: Medical fraternity must bridge urban-rural healthcare gaps: LG Sinha
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 14: Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Wednesday urged the medical fraternity to bridge the urban-rural healthcare gaps. Congratulating Government Medical College (GMC), Srinagar, for organising a conference on 'Advancing Internal Medicine: From Evidence to Excellence in Clinical Practice', LG Sinha said, “Medical science is making historic advances, and new drugs and diagnostic tools have opened up new possibilities for treatment. The greatest need today is to ensure that these innovations are not available only to physicians in large cities, but also reach doctors in villages. We must ensure that there is not even the slightest gap between urban and rural areas in access to facilities and available tools. This should be the first objective of this conference.” He underscored the critical role of internal medicine in delivering holistic and patient-centric healthcare. The LG said that physicians often face the challenging task of identifying complex underlying health conditions from seemingly simple symptoms. He said that the strength of internal medicine lies in its ability to view the human body as an interconnected system and to understand the complete medical story of a patient through clinical knowledge, experience and careful observation. LG Sinha said that observation, reason, human understanding, and courage remain the defining qualities of a physician. He said that physicians frequently serve as the first point of medical contact for families and, in many cases, build enduring relationships across generations, rooted in trust, compassion, and scientific evidence. The LG lauded GMC Srinagar for its significant contribution to medical education and healthcare, noting that generations of doctors trained by the institution continue to serve across Jammu Kashmir and the country. He also highlighted the emerging healthcare challenges. “While infectious diseases remain a concern, lifestyle-related disorders such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, fatty liver disease and cardiovascular ailments are assuming epidemic proportions. We need to ensure that advances in diagnostics, therapeutics and medical technologies reach physicians and patients in rural and remote areas as effectively as they do in urban centres,” LG Sinha said. He also called upon the medical fraternity to strengthen indigenous research and generate evidence relevant to India’s diverse population. The LG said that the country’s demographic diversity, combined with the expertise and commitment of doctors, presents immense opportunities for scientific discovery and innovation. He also outlined a five-year roadmap and proposed six key commitments for the medical community including expanding access to advanced medical knowledge through digital health platforms and telemedicine, prioritising preventive healthcare and early detection of diseases, using technology and artificial intelligence as supportive tools while preserving clinical judgement, continuously strengthening research capacity, ensuring the wellbeing of doctors and addressing professional burnout and preserving human compassion at the centre of healthcare delivery. LG Sinha urged the young doctors to remain curious, embrace innovation and learn from experienced mentors. He called upon senior physicians to generously share their clinical wisdom and guide the next generation of healthcare professionals. “Early detection of diabetes, hypertension and liver disease is less costly and can help reduce treatment expenses. I urge all physicians and internists to lead prevention campaigns at the community level, because a doctor’s voice can have an extraordinary influence on society. I have every confidence that people will take your advice seriously when it comes to preventing lifestyle-related diseases," the LG said. "We must value physicians’ hard work, service and dedication. Along with caring for patients, hospitals and institutions, it should be ensured that doctors are cared for too. Providing them with better workplaces and working conditions should be a priority.”

stories.headline: Business Not at Ease
stories.title: Business Not at Ease
stories.summary: Prescript: The World Bank which developed the concept of the Ease of Doing Business in 2003 officially discontinued it in 2021 because of major data manipulations. During 2024-2026, the Bank rolled out a redesigned framework, Business Ready (B-READY) which shifts the focus from narrow regulatory checkboxes to evaluating a country’s business environment, balancing the ease of commercial operations with public interest protections like environmental sustainability and labour rights. Historically placed in the lowest tier of “Emerging Business Ecosystems” in India, J&K climbed rather dramatically to 5th rank in the Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) in 2025. It was designated as a Top Achiever by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade at the national Udyog Samagam after scoring top marks in 4 out of 5 critical reform categories. Spurred on by this success, the government introduced the J&K Ease of Doing Business Act, 2026. The Bill, which was endorsed by industry, trade and commerce bodies, has generated a well-informed debate among diverse stakeholders. Ideally, such a bill should have been put out for formal public consultation instead of taking an internal departmental route with a compressed legislative timetable. In the context of this debate, it might be useful to spell out that Ease of Doing Business is a horizontal clearance law. It is about reducing the time, cost and uncertainty of complying with rules that already exist; licences, inspections, information demands, timelines for decisions. EoDB sets the procedural floor. The directional ceiling will, hopefully, be set in the forthcoming Industrial Policy, 2026–35. It will identify priority sectors or activities, offers capital subsidies, tax or GST-linked benefits, interest subvention, land on preferential terms, or infrastructure. The distinction is important because a lot of what is applauded or apprehended from the EODB is neither its remit nor a consequence. Much of the public anxiety and expectation is from the wrong instrument. The J&K Ease of Doing Business Act, 2026, complies with the Centre’s Deregulation 2.0 push. As a result, the structure of the local economy and the nature of business activity have not shaped the design and contents of the J&K EoDB. Instead of making an EODB relevant for Kashmir’s businesses, the working policy has been plagiarised from the Punjab EoDB Act. Punjab and Kashmir are chalk and cheese. One is a diversified economy with a broad manufacturing base and excellent market connectivity, and the other is a landlocked services-heavy, driven by horticulture and crafts with a thin micro-scale industrial sector. In Punjab, what impairs the ease of doing business are classic industrial speed breakers: factory licences, building approvals, inspections and land-use changes. The businesses in Kashmir, on the other hand, faces different binding constraints because most of the value and employment comes from primary production and services. Also, it is the informal household sector and not the estates and park-based enterprises that is driving businesses. To put it starkly, the EoDB is designed to helps a factory that is waiting on a building or trade licence. It does nothing for an orchardist whose constraint is a truck that has to clear the Banihal axis in time. Not a word about easing exports or negating the cost of being landlocked. In short, EoDB ought to have followed the actual structure of production, employment and trade of the local economy. Easing business is not only in relation to governmental intervention and interface but also alleviate structural constraints. A region specific EoDB law will still be primarily a process statute, but its definitions, tracks, timelines and supporting provisions will be relevant for the local economy. Of course, clearance delays matter in Kashmir too. But for a majority of business the unease comes from logistics, seasonal access, and land scarcity. While the EoDB speeds permissions, and sets rules to reduce bureaucratic delays, what it leaves completely unattended is the nature of business, local ownership, size class of business, and ESG. These are relevant and hence sensitive. For instance, anyone who files a Declaration of Intent is treated the same, whether a Srinagar workshop, a Jammu trader or an outside investor. There is no local-founder preference, no differential land term, no reserved park plots, and no scoring of proposals by local ownership. The preference for locals in employment that the EoDB has is enabling rather than operative. The Executive Committee may order that every enterprise with more than 10 employees to reserve a percentage of vacancies for domicile candidates. But without fixing any percentage in the Bill. Worse still, units with 10 or fewer workers which is the bulk of J&K establishments are outside even this power. Better to keep the employment-reservation power but make the percentage and the exemption process statutory and uniform and exempt local enterprises below a turnover threshold. In some instances, like the deemed registration of doctors and third-party certifiers already registered in another state or UT, makes outside professionals easier to use, not local ones. Why? The idea and intent have to be to give local enterprises concrete process benefits. Local enterprises being ones with majority ownership or control is by domicile individuals, cooperatives or producer companies. For example, priority in the 7- or 10-day tracks when capacity or plots are limited, or a longer inspection moratorium; four years instead of three. There has to be policy signalling. In addition to ownership, the EoDB simplifications should be stratified by size. Kashmir industry is overwhelmingly micro; it contributes 60 percent of industrial investment and close to 90 percent of industrial employment. The Bill must have size tools. This could include introducing a turnover band, a micro-versus-medium fee, no working-capital or inspection rule scaled to a 2-to-10-person workshop. Third, a lighter path should be created for a household enterprise as against a park-based plants. The fast lane in the EoDB Act is location: an approved industrial park gets three days; a unit outside waits ten times more! In a place where most units are not in parks, the size structure of the business and the speed structure of the Bill point in different directions. Fourth, a big fillip could have been given to logistics, which doesn’t even find a mention in the bill. The District Empowered Committee, for instance, could be empowered to have an “access protocol”; priority movement windows, coordination with security forces, traffic and disaster authorities. This will ensure export goods movement (and closures) are managed by rule rather than ad-hoc orders of security forces. The instances of apples rotting on the road because of security forces’ movement are too many to recount. Finally, environment in the EoDB is a retained constraint, not an incentive. That is deregulation of process, not a green preference. To go green has to be incentivised by fast tracking operational permissions, provide renewable-energy setoffs, give longer moratorium for effluent or energy standards and emissions. These clauses remain inside a process statute: they accelerate and structurally favour the home-grown businesses and land-efficient projects that the local economy needs. Postscript: Domain experts have red flagged the EoDB Act enabling executive relaxations to bypass statutory Master Plans which risk environmental vulnerability. Valid as these concerns may be, they demand serious introspection, not shooting the messenger as has been done by the industry bodies. Despite elaborate master plans, beginning with the Srinagar Master Plan 1971–91 nearly fifty years ago, the city has seen only haphazard growth, illegal colonies, encroachments on government land, and development in flood-prone or ecologically sensitive areas. What gives? Their practical contribution has been marginal because of implementation and enforcement shortfalls. The contention is not to support wanton development but to introspect how master plans should be redone as living, enforceable frameworks that protect Kashmir’s fragile ecology and mitigate disaster risks. Rigid paper blueprints, as the Master plans have been, are meant to be bypassed. The author is a Contributing Editor of Greater Kashmir.

Finally, environment in the EoDB is a retained constraint, not an incentive.
That is deregulation of process, not a green preference.
To go green has to be incentivised by fast tracking operational permissions, provide renewable-energy setoffs, give longer moratorium for effluent or energy standards and emissions.
These clauses remain inside a process statute: they accelerate and structurally favour the home-grown businesses and land-efficient projects that the local economy needs.
Postscript: Domain experts have red flagged the EoDB Act enabling executive relaxations to bypass statutory Master Plans which risk environmental vulnerability.
Valid as these concerns may be, they demand serious introspection, not shooting the messenger as has been done by the industry bodies.

Despite elaborate master plans, beginning with the Srinagar Master Plan 1971–91 nearly fifty years ago, the city has seen only haphazard growth, illegal colonies, encroachments on government land, and development in flood-prone or ecologically sensitive areas.
What gives?
Their practical contribution has been marginal because of implementation and enforcement shortfalls.

The contention is not to support wanton development but to introspect how master plans should be redone as living, enforceable frameworks that protect Kashmir’s fragile ecology and mitigate disaster risks.
Rigid paper blueprints, as the Master plans have been, are meant to be bypassed.
The author is a Contributing Editor of Greater Kashmir.

sentences.text: Historically placed in the lowest tier of “Emerging Business Ecosystems” in India, J&K climbed rather dramatically to 5th rank in the Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) in 2025.
Prescript: The World Bank which developed the concept of the Ease of Doing Business in 2003 officially discontinued it in 2021 because of major data manipulations.

During 2024-2026, the Bank rolled out a redesigned framework, Business Ready (B-READY) which shifts the focus from narrow regulatory checkboxes to evaluating a country’s business environment, balancing the ease of commercial operations with public interest protections like environmental sustainability and labour rights.
The J&K Ease of Doing Business Act, 2026, complies with the Centre’s Deregulation 2.0 push.
